scams.name: Adelaide Taxi Short-Run Overcharge
scams.location: Adelaide Airport taxi rank, CBD (King William, Rundle Mall), North Terrace hotel ranks
scams.tldr: Adelaide taxis stack undisclosed surcharges — fuel fees, airport levies, late-night rates — onto metered fares to push a $28 airport-to-CBD trip to $65 or more, targeting arriving tourists who do not know the local rate.
scams.description:
You land at Adelaide Airport and join the taxi queue for the 7-km trip to your North Terrace hotel. The cab looks official; the driver starts the meter. The ride proceeds without comment.

At drop-off the meter shows $65 for what Uber quotes at $28. The driver itemizes surcharges: a fuel levy, an airport fee, and an unspecified late-night rate — none disclosed before the trip. Some drivers use tampered meters that click in $0.40 increments instead of the legal rate.

Use Uber or DiDi from the Adelaide Airport rideshare bay for a price-locked CBD fare of $25–$40. Adelaide Metro JetExpress buses (J1, J2, J3) run from the airport to the CBD for $5.40 with a Metrocard — the cheapest scam-proof option. If you take a taxi, watch the meter display, pay by card, and photograph the plate and driver ID before the trip in case you need to file a complaint.

scams.name: DiDi / Uber 'Cancel Mid-Trip' Charge Scam
scams.location: Adelaide CBD, DiDi and Uber platform
scams.tldr: DiDi drivers in Adelaide's CBD fake a completed pickup — pulling up, waiting thirty seconds, then moving 100 metres and ending the trip in the app — charging a $15 "cancellation/part-trip fee" while you are still standing on the pavement.
scams.description:
You book a DiDi from Rundle Mall to the Adelaide Oval — a $9 trip. A car appears on the map, the driver pins the pickup point, and the app shows "driver arriving."

The driver pulls up, waits thirty seconds, then moves 100 metres down the road and ends the ride in the app. Your card is charged $15 for a "cancellation fee" and "part-trip fare." The driver collects a full payout and moves on. A related variant has the driver claiming an "app issue" and asking you to pay in cash directly.

If a driver ends your trip before reaching you, immediately screenshot the ride, then dispute it in-app citing the trip-end location discrepancy. For any cash-payment request citing "app issues," cancel the ride, book a different driver, and report the first driver's details. Escalate to a credit card chargeback if the platform's response stalls.

scams.name: Fake Barossa / McLaren Vale Wine Tour Booking
scams.location: Online via Google Ads, Facebook Ads, cloned tour booking sites
scams.tldr: Cloned tour-operator websites and Facebook Marketplace listings offer Barossa Valley wine tours at $79 per person with bank-transfer-only payment — no minibus arrives on tour day and the phone number disconnects.
scams.description:
You search "Barossa wine tour from Adelaide" and a polished site ranks high on the results: full-day tour, four wineries, lunch included, hotel pickup, $79. The photos are professional and the reviews look legitimate.

The booking instructions ask you to pay by bank transfer "to avoid card fees." You transfer $79–$160 per person. On tour day, no minibus arrives. The phone goes to voicemail and is eventually disconnected. The site was cloned from a legitimate operator's design, placed on a different domain, and boosted by Google Ads to outrank the genuine listing.

Book Barossa and McLaren Vale tours only through verified operators with Australian Business Numbers listed at abn.business.gov.au — and always pay by credit card. Established operators include Groovy Grape Tours (groovygrape.com.au), Taste the Barossa, and Barossa Daimler. A bank transfer or PayPal Friends & Family request for a tour booking is an immediate scam signal.

scams.name: Adelaide Fake Rental / Facebook Airbnb Invoice Scam
scams.location: CBD, North Adelaide, Unley, Prospect — short-stay and sharehouse market
scams.tldr: Scammers on Facebook Marketplace list Adelaide short-stay apartments, then send official-looking Airbnb invoice PDFs requesting a bank transfer — the booking does not exist in Airbnb's system and the money is unrecoverable.
scams.description:
You find a one-bedroom apartment in North Adelaide on Facebook Marketplace for $120 per night. The listing has photos, a friendly "host," and quick response times. The host says they manage bookings directly to keep rates lower.

They send a convincing Airbnb-branded invoice PDF for the full stay — $840 — and ask you to bank-transfer the amount to "confirm the booking." You pay. No Airbnb confirmation email arrives because there is no booking: Airbnb has no record of the listing, the host, or the transaction. The scammers vanish as soon as the transfer clears.

A real Airbnb booking is confirmed only inside the Airbnb app — any "invoice PDF" requesting a bank transfer is a scam regardless of how official it looks. Book short stays exclusively through the Airbnb app or a bookmarked airbnb.com.au URL. If you have already transferred money, call your bank within 24 hours and request a recall.

scams.name: International Student Visa / Education Agent Fraud
scams.location: Online / WeChat / WhatsApp ads targeting South Asian and Southeast Asian students
scams.tldr: Migration agents advertising on social media in Adelaide charge $8,000–$13,000 for "guaranteed PR pathways" through unaccredited colleges — they enrol victims in non-existent courses and disappear with the upfront cash payment.
scams.description:
You are a prospective international student or recent graduate in Adelaide. A "migration agent" advertising on Instagram or WeChat offers a visa pathway or PR sponsorship through an Adelaide-based college, at a price far below formal immigration firms. The agent is plausible, responsive, and references real visa categories.

The agent takes $8,000–$13,000 upfront in cash, enrolls you in a course at an unregistered or non-CRICOS college, and then becomes uncontactable. The visa pathway does not exist, the enrollment is worthless, and the course fees cannot be recovered. Victims often delay reporting because of embarrassment or fear of immigration consequences.

Only use MARA-registered migration agents — verify registration at mara.gov.au before paying anything, and check that any college is listed on cricos.education.gov.au. Never pay cash for visa or education services; always pay by card or bank transfer to a registered ABN with a receipt. Any "guaranteed PR" promise is a lie — no legitimate agent can guarantee visa outcomes.

scams.name: Fake 'SA Tourism Voucher' / Booking Voucher Scam
scams.location: Email / SMS / Facebook ads claiming South Australian government tourism vouchers
scams.tldr: Phishing emails impersonating the South Australian Tourism Commission offer $100 hotel vouchers, then direct recipients to a cloned site that harvests credit card details — the voucher never materializes and small unauthorized charges follow.
scams.description:
You receive an email claiming a "South Australian Tourism Commission" voucher worth $100 off any winter hotel stay. The branding looks official — it uses SATC's logo, fonts, and color scheme — and the offer is timely enough to feel credible.

The link leads to a cloned site resembling southaustralia.com. It asks for your name, email, and credit card details to "verify your voucher." You enter the card. The voucher never arrives; within days, small test transactions appear followed by larger unauthorized charges. Scammers used the SA government's real "Great State Voucher" program (2020–2022) as a plausible brand to impersonate on an ongoing basis.

Never click a voucher link in an email or SMS — go directly to southaustralia.com or tourism.sa.gov.au to verify whether any voucher program is currently active. Real SA government promotions are announced on official .gov.au domains. Report phishing attempts to ScamWatch at scamwatch.gov.au and contact your bank immediately if you have already entered card details.
